boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Caldiero entry (29-31 October 1805) in cohort v1's third-coalition 1805 group: Masséna's Army of Italy against Archduke Charles's army before and at the entrenched position of Caldiero, from side A's advance out of Verona on 29 October, including the fighting in the Monti Lessini against Rosenberg's division that both accounts treat as part of the battle, through the main day of the 30th (Colognola, Caldiero, Gombione and Sabbionara) to the fighting of the 31st at Gombione and Chiavicca del Christo. claims.value: Side B (Austrian), side A's figures: Koch gives the Austrian position after the 29th as the right under Simbschen, 20 battalions and 4 squadrons, on the heights of Colognola and San Pietro; the centre under Bellegarde, 16 battalions and 12 squadrons, supported on the chaussée by a reserve of 14 battalions and 12 squadrons, on the heights of San Mathia and la Rocca and in the entrenchments of Ponterotto; on the left 14 battalions and 8 squadrons at Madonna di Stra under the Prince of Reuss, 8 battalions and 7 squadrons at Chiavica del Cristo and a battalion in the entrenchments of Ponte-Zerpan; and 7 battalions and 8 squadrons under Argenteau in reserve at San Gregorio: in all 49,200 combattants under the Archduke's hand. Koch says detachments sent to Germany over the previous fortnight had reduced the Archduke's army to under 50,000 men; before the fighting on the Adige began he gives the Austrian army facing Masséna as 83,414 men.
claims.rationale: Side A's history on side B, read from the page images; Koch gives no source for these figures. His units add up to 80 battalions and 51 squadrons (our sum), against Angeli's 79 and 52. The deployment was the Archduke's for his attack of the 30th (claim side-b-command), so the claim is tagged commander_created; the 83,414 is the army before Verona, not the force at Caldiero. English renderings (ours): 'the general position of the Austrians was thus settled: the right wing under General Simbschen, 20 battalions and 4 squadrons strong, occupied the heights of Colognola and San Pietro'; 'the centre, under Bellegarde, of 16 battalions and 12 squadrons, supported on the chaussée by a reserve of 14 battalions and 12 squadrons, was formed on the heights of San Mathia and la Rocca as well as in the entrenchments of Ponterotto, covering the outlets of Caldiero, the reserve astride the chaussée'; 'the left had 14 battalions and 8 squadrons posted at Madonna di Stra under the orders of the Prince of Reuss, 8 battalions and 7 squadrons at Chiavica del Cristo, and a battalion in the entrenchments of Ponte-Zerpan. 7 battalions and 8 squadrons commanded by Count Argenteau formed a reserve in the camp of San Gregorio'; 'all the forces thus united under Prince Charles's hand came to 49,200 combatants'; 'although, as a result of the detachments he had been sending to Germany for a fortnight, his army was reduced to less than 50,000 men'; 'thus the two armies, the first 41,355 men strong and the second 83,414 (see pièces justificatives, no. claims.value: Side A (French), its own figures: Koch's order of battle of the Army of Italy at the time of 18 October 1805 gives its field divisions as 77 battalions and 59 squadrons, 41,355 men (right wing 27 battalions, 10 squadrons, 11,195 men; centre 13 battalions, 6,812; left wing 29 battalions, 7 squadrons, 14,840; reserve 8 battalions, 15 squadrons, 3,949; cavalry 27 squadrons, 4,559), not counting 5,733 in garrisons, 5,240 in hospital and 12,907 in the depots, an effective of 65,235, with 54 field guns. For the main attack Masséna assembled the divisions of Gardanne, Duhesme, Molitor, Partonneaux and Espagne before Vago to attack the centre, while Seras's division, facing the Trentino corps and Rosenberg, guarded the outlets of Monte Baldo. For the last day his order to Verdier left the 4th and 19th chasseurs in observation on the lower Adige.
claims.rationale: Side A's return, printed by Koch and read from the page images, with Koch's narrative of the assembly (OCR). claims.value: Masséna commanded side A and decided to attack: weary of the indecisive situation, Koch says, he resolved to take the initiative himself, and Angeli that he went over to the attack with his own impetuosity. His plan, long settled, was to break the Austrian centre with the mass of his forces, turn the Austrian left and throw it into the marshes of Arcole, but first to force the Archduke by a serious action to deploy. On the 29th Seras, leaving a brigade between the Adige and Lake Garda, crossed the Adige at Pescantina; Duhesme and Gardanne crossed at Castel Vecchio and Duhesme attacked the entrenchments of San Dionigio; Molitor attacked the Austrian advanced posts before the position. For the next day Masséna ordered Verdier to cross at Perzacco at daybreak, force the Austrian extreme left and seize the river dyke. Taking the sound of Brun's fight for Verdier's crossing, he shifted the weight of the attack onto the Austrian centre and left (Angeli). Seeing the danger from Bellegarde's column, he sent a division of artillery against its flank, ordered Gardanne to hold firm astride the road, and sent Espagne and Partonneaux against its flanks (Koch). Having used all his reserves, he returned to his first plan: Gardanne to hold the enemy at Caldiero, Molitor to storm the heights of Colognola (Angeli). Wishing to unite all his forces for the next day, he ordered Verdier to finish crossing at Zevio and join Duhesme on the right (Koch); after reports of threatening movements on his flanks he drew his army together around Vago (Angeli).
claims.rationale: Side A's decisions at the battle from Koch, written from Masséna's papers, and Angeli (page images except the passages marked OCR below; the date and hour in Koch's sentences are not restated). English renderings (ours): Koch, 'at last on ... (OCR) October, the bridgehead being built and armed, Masséna, weary of this indecisive situation so contrary to his impetuous character, resolved to put an end to it by taking the initiative himself' (OCR); Angeli, 'weary of the enforced inactivity, Masséna went over to the attack with his own impetuosity' (OCR); Koch, 'the marshal's plan, though subject to circumstances, had long been settled: to break through the centre with the mass of his forces, to turn the enemy left, cut it off and throw it into the marshes of Arcole. But so as not to engage rashly, he had by a serious action to force the Archduke to deploy his troops'; 'accordingly on the 29th, at four in the morning, General Seras left a brigade to guard the gap between the Adige and Lake Garda, crossed the river at Pescantina in large boats and threw a bridge at Polo under the protection of his artillery'; Angeli, 'on the ... (OCR) at daybreak the divisions Duhesme and Gardanne passed the bridge at Castel Vecchio and pushed the outposts back on their supports' (OCR); Koch, 'Duhesme vigorously attacked the entrenchments of San Dionigio' (OCR); 'Molitor went onto the height and vigorously attacked the Austrian advanced posts' (OCR); 'Masséna for his part ordered General Verdier to cross the Adige at Perzacco at daybreak, force the enemy's extreme left and occupy the river dyke' (OCR); Angeli, 'which led the French commander into the mistaken opinion that Verdier had already carried out the river crossing' (OCR); 'on this assumption Masséna believed the moment for the decisive thrust had come, which however required a change of the plan of attack settled so far, in that he now shifted the weight of the action onto the centre and the left wing of the Austrian army' (OCR); Koch, 'Masséna sees the danger; he has a division of artillery brought up at the gallop on the flank of this formidable column, and orders Gardanne to hold firm astride the road, and General Espagne to come onto the left flank with one of his brigades, which will find room there, while General Partonneaux moves onto the right flank at the double' (OCR); Angeli, 'Masséna had now used up all his reserves without being nearer the goal than in the morning' (OCR); 'Gardanne was to continue the advance against Caldiero and hold the enemy there, but Molitor to storm the heights of Colognola, break the right wing of the Austrian position and then roll up the position itself' (OCR); Koch, 'the fight should have begun again the next day; but Masséna, wishing to unite all his forces to make it decisive, sent Verdier the order to finish his crossing at Zevio and to join the division Duhesme on the right wing by the chaussée of Bendinara'; Angeli, as in claim side-a-information for the reports and Vago.

claims.value: Archduke Charles commanded side B. Koch says the offensive was forbidden him, so that he was to fight only for the security of his retreat, and that he chose the entrenched position of Caldiero to receive the battle. During the night after the fighting of the 29th he drew Wetzel's brigade, Vogelsang with the grenadier brigades of Lippa and Hohenlohe, and the regiments Archduke Charles uhlans and Savoy dragoons forward into the position for his attack, and his disposition sent Simbschen from Colognola alta against Lavagno, Bellegarde's 2nd column, under the Archduke's personal direction, along the chaussée against Vago, and Reuss and Nordmann against side A's right flank and rear. The very unfavourable weather made him hold back the middle columns; when he heard firing on his left he attacked, Bellegarde advancing along the chaussée against Strà. When side A's skirmishers followed his retreating infantry close up to the works, he had Vogelsang advance from the reserve with Lippa's grenadiers and the regiment Eszterházy and led them forward in person (Angeli; Koch has him put himself at the head of Vogelsang's grenadiers, supported by Esterhazy's regiment). He sent grenadier support to Colognola and ordered Bellegarde to go there, but Simbschen's dispositions had already largely averted the danger. When Lenchantin's brigade had pushed beyond Caldiero he launched Hohenlohe's grenadier brigade from the reserve behind the position, while Archduke Maximilian led the rallied battalions forward again. On the 31st, after Nordmann was badly wounded, Colloredo took command and brought up the reserves, and Reuss threw a regiment with several hundred Croats on Verdier's right flank and sent a strong column of Hungarian grenadiers toward Gombione (Koch). After Bubna brought the official news of the disaster at Ulm, the Archduke resolved to break free at any price and retreat, and so to attack side A's left the following day and force it into full retreat (Angeli).

claims.value: Bodart places side B (Austrian) under Archduke Charles in the left column of his table, the winner's place by his stated rule, so he records a victory of side B over side A (French). Angeli agrees: the battle ended with Masséna's retreat, and in Angeli's judgment Masséna, after the experience of the last days, could well prefer to clear the battlefield of his own accord rather than risk a renewed clash; on the night of the 30th side B pursued side A only as far as Strà and its troops stayed under arms on the battlefield; the Archduke's relation speaks of the victory of Caldiero, and his army order of 4 November says all the enemy's attacks were repulsed until, after three days of fruitless effort, the enemy gave up hope of beating the army and withdrew with considerable loss. Angeli adds that the battle did not end with a vigorous pursuit and the enemy's repulse over the Adige, but led directly to the conditions the Archduke needed for his further plans.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome (side A lost), read from Bodart's table and rules, with the statements of side B's account (page images except the passages marked OCR). Koch's account calls the main day indecisive (claim koch-indecisive). Bodart also states a rule for so-called indecisive battles; the passages read do not say whether he applied it here. English renderings (ours): Bodart, 'the winner's place in the comparisons is always to be sought on the left side, the loser's on the right'; 'in so-called indecisive battles the party regarded as winner was the one that held the battlefield or achieved the purpose sought by the fight, even if its material loss was greater'; the table as in claim bodart-commanders; Angeli, 'after the experiences of the last days Masséna could in any case prefer to clear the battlefield voluntarily rather than expose himself to the vicissitudes of a renewed clash'; 'with Masséna's retreat this remarkable battle ended, in which both opponents had given proofs of heroic endurance and of a bravery above all praise'; 'Archduke Charles had the beaten enemy pursued only as far as Strà, where the dark night at last called a halt to the fight' (OCR); 'the Austrian troops stayed under arms on the battlefield through the night' (OCR); '"wherever", says Archduke Charles in his relation, "the service of Your Majesty requires the use of this army, the victory of Caldiero stands at its side and will be its watchword in future undertakings"'; 'the excellent conduct of the imperial troops found its deserved recognition first in the army order dated headquarters Fontaniva, 4 November (F. A. XIII, 114½), which reads:'; 'all the enemy's attacks, which were undertaken with much bravery, were repulsed and frustrated, until he himself at last, after three days of fruitless labour, gave up hope of defeating the army and withdrew with considerable loss'; 'if the battle of Caldiero did not end with a vigorous pursuit of the enemy and his being driven back over the Adige, it nonetheless led directly to such conditions as Archduke Charles had judged necessary and aimed at for his further plans' (OCR).

claims.value: Koch calls the 30th, the battle's main day, an indecisive and bloody day with balanced losses. In his account Gardanne, having reached the foot of the entrenchments, was stopped by the dark night and bivouacked on the ground won, and the engagement of the 31st, by delaying the junction of Verdier's and Duhesme's divisions by a day, gave the Archduke the leisure to carry out his retreat, which began on 1 November. Angeli, while treating the battle as a success for side B, also writes that despite the sacrifices of both sides the battle of the 30th had not essentially changed the state of affairs.
claims.rationale: Koch's word 'indécise' gives a different result from Bodart's victory of side B (claim bodart-winner), so it is kept as a dispute and not resolved. Koch and Angeli also differ on how the 30th ended: Koch has Gardanne, after being driven out of Caldiero by Hohenlohe's grenadiers and attacking twice more, bivouac on the ground won at the foot of the works, Angeli has side A driven back to Strà and Masséna withdraw to the line Gombioni-Ca Rizzi-Ca dell'Ara. English renderings (ours): Koch, 'the losses were balanced on this indecisive and bloody day'; '[Gar]danne, after overthrowing the regiment of Esterhazy, putting General Lippa out of action and breaking his grenadiers, carried the village at the bayonet' (OCR), 'but was driven out by the Prince of Hohenlohe at the head of 5 battalions of grenadiers. After two more attacks he had at last reached the foot of the entrenchments, which the brigade Lenchantin was passing on the high road, when the night, already very dark, forced him to halt his movement and bivouac on the ground won'; 'this engagement, by delaying by a day the junction of the divisions Verdier and Duhesme, gave Prince Charles the leisure to carry out his retreat, which began on 1 November, at four in the afternoon, in 3 columns'; Angeli, 'despite the sacrifices made by both sides, the battle of ... (OCR) October had not essentially changed the state of affairs' (OCR); 'Masséna withdrew to the line Gombioni-Ca Rizzi-Ca dell'Ara' (OCR).

claims.value: Bodart describes Caldiero as a market town in Venetia, 15 km east of Verona. The Austrian position filled the whole space between the Adige and the western Monti Lessini: its right wing was the ridge on which Colognola lies, from the deep, steep ravine of Bocca Scalucce to the isolated knolls of S. Matia and la Rocca, between which the Verona-Vicenza road ran; from there the front continued over the plain to Chiavicca del Christo on the Adige, with the village of Caldiero in front of it (Angeli). Koch gives the position as 7,000 m long, shortening the line of the Adige, with a view over the enemy's movements from the bell tower of Colognola. The foreground favoured the defence: cut by ditches and hedges and covered with buildings and trees, it hindered attacking columns on the right, and the terraced slope from Monte Zovo to Bocca Scalucce was a serious obstacle; on the left the flat ground toward the Strada Porcilana and the rice fields allowed cavalry, but toward the Adige troops were tied to the roads and dykes; the many scattered stone farmhouses suited defence (Angeli). Fog covered the field on the morning of the 30th, and on the 31st side B's troops on the narrow dyke roads were fired on from the rice fields.

claims.value: Before the battle the Archduke rid his army of everything that limited its freedom of manoeuvre, which roads ruined by constant rain made urgent: the guns of one calibre, except those kept on the right wing, and the centre's artillery reserve, except the cavalry guns, were sent back to Vicenza and only the ammunition needed for immediate use was kept (Angeli); after Ulm he had supplies of every kind moved from Palma Nova to Venice and those he would need on his retreat sent to Laybach (Koch). In the centre, Bellegarde's battalions, attacked in front and on the flanks and tired from the long fight, were partly out of ammunition (Angeli). On the 29th the fatigue of side A's troops and nightfall made Masséna put off the decisive attack (Koch, Angeli); general exhaustion kept both sides quiet the next forenoon (Angeli). Rosenberg's troops, marching on mountain paths to join the battle, lacked footwear and food (Angeli).

claims.value: Before the battle the news of Ulm's capitulation and of the destruction of the Austrian army in Germany reached side A's headquarters by way of Switzerland (Angeli). Masséna knew precisely, Angeli says, that the Archduke had been much weakened by detachments to Germany, but would not commit himself before he had forced the Archduke to deploy and so gained a basis for his final dispositions; Koch gives the same intention. Angeli says the fighting of the 29th let Masséna reconnoitre the Austrian positions more closely, and Koch that it partly fulfilled his views, the Archduke having been obliged to deploy. On the 30th fog hid the field; Masséna took the sound of Brun's fight with Nordmann for Verdier's crossing (Angeli), and when the fog fell side A saw enemy columns coming out of the entrenchments (Koch). After the last day's fighting Serras, misled by Hillinger's advance, reported a movement of Rosenberg's against Veronetta, while reports came from the right of Davidovich's demonstrations and of the occupation of Isola Porcarizza; though not in doubt about the Archduke's final intentions, Masséna judged it wiser to draw his army together around Vago. Angeli says these were the circumstances that, according to French sources, led Masséna to concentrate to the rear.

claims.value: Koch says the Archduke, enlightened by recent events, supposed that Masséna would attempt the decisive crossing at Verona. In the forenoon of the 29th the Archduke learned of side A's attacks together with reports of troop movements along the whole lower Adige; because ground covered with trees and crops hid side A's movements and strength, its intentions were not yet clear, and he kept the centre ready to march and sent Wetzel's brigade toward the right; Davidovich then reported that strong detachments were being drawn from the lower Adige to Verona (Angeli). Koch says the demonstrations made the Archduke move his headquarters to San Bonifacio and keep him from stripping his centre or left; Angeli replies that the Archduke was far from intimidated and that side A's thrusts ripened his plan to attack. Austrian headquarters was convinced a general attack was imminent: reports from the left of troops marching up the Adige and of outposts withdrawn, and the many campfires before the front, let it expect side A's united forces the next day (Angeli). Bubna, sent by the Emperor, arrived from Vienna with the official news of the disaster at Ulm (Angeli); Koch places the news of the reverses in Germany after the fighting of the 30th. After the 30th the Archduke as yet had no news of Rosenberg; after the last day's fighting his headquarters still expected a fourth day of battle, and at dawn it saw that side A had left the field (Angeli).

claims.value: Both sides attacked. Side A opened the battle: on the 29th Seras crossed the Adige above Verona, Duhesme and Gardanne crossed at Castel Vecchio against the Austrian troops in the hills, the other divisions forced the Austrian advanced guard at S. Michele back on the position, and Molitor attacked the advanced troops before the position, side A establishing itself in Strà and even Caldiero at dusk; on the 30th it attacked Colognola, Caldiero and the Austrian left at Gombione and Sabbionara, and on the 31st Verdier and Duhesme attacked the Austrian left up to the works of Chiavicca del Christo. Side B attacked on the 30th: the Archduke had resolved to break out of his position and throw side A back over the Adige, and his plan was a thrust from both wings with the main attack, which he meant to lead himself, toward Caldiero and Vago; when firing began on his left he attacked, and Bellegarde's column advanced along the chaussée and forced side A out of Strà. Koch says the Archduke sent four columns out of the entrenchments to threaten side A's flanks and ease the advance of his centre on the chaussée.
claims.rationale: Both accounts describe main attacks by each side on the 30th, so the code is both_attacked; side B's attack of the 30th was planned as a sortie to throw side A back over the Adige, not a counterattack inside its position. The counterattacks at Colognola and by Hohenlohe's grenadiers were inside the position and do not by themselves make side B an attacker. Angeli also writes that the French were everywhere the attackers and that in each decisive action the Austrians fought a superior attacker (claims side-a-losses-reported and angeli-side-a); this is kept in the record. Both commanders at the battle decided to attack (claims side-a-command and side-b-command), so the posture is tagged commander_created, although Koch says the offensive was forbidden the Archduke from above. claims.value: Side B fought from an entrenched position. Angeli calls it a position strengthened alike by nature and art, and says the Archduke had, since his arrival in Italy, raised its natural strength by extensive entrenchments: redoubts crowned the most important points of the right wing, trenches and advanced breastworks covered the slopes the redoubts could not sweep, the church and village of Colognola were prepared for defence, and on the left there were redoubts at Chiavigetto and Chiavicca del Christo and armed flèches at Ponterotto and Belfiore di Porcile, with firing steps for infantry cut in the dykes along the Adige and the Alpone; a Grenzer battalion held the work at Ponte Zerpa. Koch describes a redoubt on Monte Nafari, redoubts sweeping the Verona road and the plain of Caldiero, the church of Colognola surrounded by a good wall, a flèche at Chiavighetto and a redoubt near Ponte Ratto, a strong redoubt at Chiavica del Cristo and all houses fit for defence entrenched, and the centre in the entrenchments of Ponterotto. Side A attacked these works: on the 29th it pushed up to the trenches and was thrown back by fire from the works (Angeli); on the 30th some of its soldiers got in by the embrasures of a redoubt at Colognola and a regiment's eagles waved for a moment on the parapet before the defenders remained masters of the work (Koch); on the 31st side A advanced to the foot of the entrenchments and assailed them (Koch), and Nordmann threw part of his brigade into the redoubt at Chiavicca del Christo (Angeli). No passage read places side A in works.
claims.rationale: Koch and Angeli agree on the works, so they are recorded in one claim (OCR except Koch's pp. 94, 97 and 104 and Angeli's p. 115, read from the page images; counts of works, guns and men and regiment numbers seen only in the OCR are not restated). They are field works which, Angeli says, the Archduke, side B's commander at this battle, had laid out for this position, and Koch says he chose the entrenched position to receive the battle, so the claim is tagged commander_created; Angeli says the Archduke had given the position his greatest care since his arrival in Italy, and the passages read give no dates for the works. Most consequential gap: side A's strength at Caldiero. Koch's order of battle is for 18 October (41,355 in the field divisions), Bodart gives 46,000 and Angeli 45,000; no passage read gives the divisions' strength on 29-31 October or says which divisions Bodart counted (Seras's division faced the Trentino and Rosenberg, and for the last day Pully's was to stay on the lower Adige). A French return for late October, such as one among Koch's pièces justificatives or in the war ministry's archives, could close it.

Disputes kept as separate claims or recorded in them: the result (Bodart's victory of side B, Angeli's 'Sieg von Caldiero', Koch's 'journée indécise'); how the 30th ended (Gardanne bivouacking on the ground won at the foot of the works, Koch; side A driven back to Strà, Angeli); side B's loss (Bodart 5,700 killed and wounded with no prisoners; Koch 5,672 for the 30th including 1,800 prisoners; Angeli 120 officers and 5552 men in all); side A's strength (Bodart 46,000; Angeli 45,000; Koch's 41,355 on 18 October); side B's battalions and squadrons (Angeli 79 and 52; Koch's units, 80 and 51 by our sum); where Gardanne was driven back to on the 30th (Koch's 'Rotta', which Angeli disputes in a footnote, OCR); where Nordmann was wounded on the 31st (in the engagement at Gombione, Koch; on the parapet of the work, Angeli, OCR); whether Verdier's demonstrations kept the Archduke from weakening his centre (Koch) or not (Angeli).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his battalions, squadrons and side B losses match Angeli's and his side A loss equals the Archduke's estimate); Koch (a French history from Masséna's papers and the war ministry's depots, printing the army's order of battle); Angeli (an Austrian history from the Kriegsarchiv, commissioned by the Archduke's family; his source notes 62-68 cite pages of Koch's volume V (page numbers read in the OCR), his footnotes answer Koch's account, and his 49,200 equals Koch's, so he is not independent of Koch for the dispositions and may not be for the losses).
